title: Central-Line Dressing Integrity: Damp, Loose, or Soiled Means Change
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Central-line dressings protect a high-risk access site. A damp, loose, visibly soiled, or nonocclusive dressing requires prompt replacement using the prescribed sterile technique and product.
recognize: Moisture, lifting edges, blood/soil, tenderness, drainage, erythema.
priorities: Inspect site/dressing and correct compromised coverage promptly.
assessMonitor: Site tenderness, erythema, drainage, dressing integrity, catheter length/securement, fever.
interventions: Use aseptic technique and facility-approved dressing-change process; keep site protected from water exposure.
medicationSafety: Do not infuse through a line with suspected infection or displacement without clinical review when an alternative is needed.
teaching: Keep dressing dry/intact and report loosening or site pain.
delegationScope: Central-line dressing changes require competency and policy authorization; abnormal findings require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Reinforcing a visibly contaminated central-line dressing indefinitely instead of changing it appropriately.
oneLinePearl: If the central-line dressing no longer protects the site, fix it now.

title: Scrub the Hub: Every Access Is an Infection-Control Event
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Central-line hubs/connectors can transmit organisms directly into the bloodstream. Perform hand hygiene and disinfect access points according to current facility/device protocol before each entry.
recognize: Repeated access, emergency manipulation, contaminated connector, poor hand hygiene increase risk.
priorities: Use aseptic access every time and minimize unnecessary line entries.
assessMonitor: Connector integrity, site findings, fever, unexplained chills during infusion.
interventions: Disinfect connector and allow antiseptic action/drying per product protocol; use sterile supplies.
medicationSafety: Never reuse contaminated syringes or connectors and never bypass hub-disinfection steps for urgency that is not life-threatening.
teaching: Patients should not manipulate hubs or caps unless specifically trained.
delegationScope: Line access is competency/policy dependent and may be restricted for PN/LVN practice.
examTrap: Skipping hub disinfection because the cap looks clean.

title: Possible CLABSI: Fever Plus a Central Line Needs Prompt Evaluation
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A central-line patient with fever, chills, unexplained hypotension, line tenderness, or purulent drainage requires prompt infection/sepsis evaluation. Do not assume the line is innocent because the site looks normal.
recognize: Rigors during infusion, fever without clear source, local tenderness, drainage, hemodynamic change.
priorities: Assess sepsis severity and notify RN/provider; follow orders for cultures and line management.
assessMonitor: Vitals, site, blood cultures/labs as ordered, infusion timing, other infection sources.
interventions: Maintain aseptic handling and prepare for ordered culture/removal/replacement plan.
medicationSafety: Administer antimicrobials as ordered; do not delay sepsis treatment while debating the source.
teaching: Report fever, chills, drainage, or new line pain promptly.
examTrap: Waiting for obvious redness before considering catheter-related bloodstream infection.
oneLinePearl: A clean-looking site does not rule out CLABSI.

title: Central-Line Occlusion: Never Force a Flush
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Resistance to flushing or inability to aspirate may reflect mechanical obstruction, malposition, precipitate, thrombotic occlusion, or clamp/tubing issues. Never force fluid through a resistant central line.
recognize: New resistance, absent blood return when expected, kink, closed clamp, positional change, swelling/pain.
priorities: Stop, inspect for external mechanical causes, and follow line-specific troubleshooting policy.
assessMonitor: Catheter position/length, clamps, tubing, arm/neck swelling, pain, infusion history.
interventions: Use only ordered/authorized declotting or troubleshooting protocols.
medicationSafety: Do not push medication into a line with unresolved resistance or uncertain placement.
teaching: Patients should report pump alarms, swelling, or discomfort immediately.
delegationScope: Central-line troubleshooting/declotting is competency and policy dependent.
examTrap: Using extra force because the line is probably just sticky.
oneLinePearl: Resistance means stop and troubleshoot—not push harder.

title: PICC/CVC Migration: External Length Change Can Mean Internal Position Change
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A change in visible catheter length, new inability to flush, pain, swelling, or rhythm symptoms can indicate migration or dislodgement. Stop use and obtain clinical review before further infusion when placement is uncertain.
recognize: More/less catheter visible, loose securement, sudden line dysfunction, arm/neck swelling, palpitations.
priorities: Stop infusion if migration is suspected, secure catheter without advancing it, notify RN/provider.
assessMonitor: External length, securement, site, arm circumference/swelling, symptoms.
medicationSafety: Do not advance a partially dislodged catheter back into the vessel.
teaching: Avoid pulling and report any visible length change.
delegationScope: Line-position decisions require qualified licensed clinicians.
examTrap: Pushing a migrated PICC back to the original mark.
oneLinePearl: Changed external length means placement must be re-verified.

title: Central-Line Thrombosis: Swelling and Pain Need Escalation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Unilateral arm/neck swelling, venous distention, pain, sluggish line function, or unexplained edema in a patient with a PICC/CVC can signal catheter-associated thrombosis.
recognize: Asymmetric swelling, discomfort, collateral veins, line dysfunction.
priorities: Stop unnecessary manipulation and notify RN/provider for diagnostic evaluation.
assessMonitor: Limb/neck swelling, pain, color, circulation, dyspnea/chest pain, line function.
medicationSafety: Do not massage the affected limb or independently start/stop anticoagulation.
teaching: Report new swelling or pain on the catheter side promptly.
examTrap: Treating arm swelling as simple dependent edema in a PICC patient.
oneLinePearl: PICC plus unilateral swelling = think thrombosis.

title: Central-Line Air Embolism: Open System Plus Sudden Symptoms Is an Emergency
bottomLine: An open or disconnected central venous system can permit air entry. Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, cough, confusion, hypoxemia, or hemodynamic change after disconnection/manipulation requires emergency response.
recognize: Disconnected hub, uncapped lumen, cracked catheter, sudden cardiopulmonary/neuro symptoms.
priorities: Clamp/occlude the open line if safe and within policy, call emergency help, support ABCs.
assessMonitor: Oxygenation, respiratory status, hemodynamics, neurologic status, line integrity.
interventions: Follow emergency air-embolism protocol and provider orders.
medicationSafety: Do not delay emergency response for routine line flushing or medication administration.
teaching: Keep all lumens securely capped/clamped as instructed.
delegationScope: Emergency management follows facility protocol; PN scope is implementation/monitoring/escalation.
examTrap: Flushing the line first to see if the symptoms improve.
oneLinePearl: Open central line plus sudden symptoms = air embolism emergency.

title: Cracked or Leaking Central Line: Stop Use and Protect the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A cracked, leaking, cut, or damaged central catheter risks blood loss, infection, air entry, and medication extravasation. Stop use and follow the device-specific emergency repair/replacement pathway.
recognize: Fluid/blood leakage, visible crack, damp dressing during infusion, catheter damage.
priorities: Stop infusion, clamp as appropriate proximal to damage per policy, notify qualified clinician.
assessMonitor: Line integrity, bleeding, symptoms, infusion type, dressing/site.
interventions: Use only approved repair or replacement procedures.
medicationSafety: Never tape over a damaged catheter and resume infusion unless a validated repair protocol specifically permits it.
teaching: Protect tubing from scissors, pets, pulling, and crushing.
delegationScope: Repair decisions are restricted to qualified personnel.
examTrap: Covering a catheter crack with tape and continuing a vesicant infusion.
oneLinePearl: Damaged central line = stop use, secure, escalate.

title: Central-Line Necessity: Every Extra Day Adds Risk
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Central venous access should remain only while clinically necessary. Ongoing need should be reviewed because unnecessary catheter days increase infection and mechanical-complication exposure.
recognize: Line no longer used, therapy complete, suitable alternate access available.
priorities: Clarify ongoing indication during handoff/rounds and escalate removal consideration to RN/provider.
assessMonitor: Current indication, frequency/type of use, complications, alternative access.
interventions: Support prompt removal when ordered and no longer needed.
medicationSafety: Do not keep a central line solely for hypothetical future medication convenience.
redFlags: No clear indication plus emerging line complication
teaching: Explain that removal when no longer needed is a safety step.
examTrap: Keeping a PICC 'just in case' after therapy ends without a current indication.
oneLinePearl: No indication means question the line.

title: Home Central-Line Safety: Clean Handling and Backup Planning
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Home central-line care depends on trained clean/aseptic handling, dry intact dressings, secure equipment, and clear plans for fever, line damage, occlusion, or pump failure.
recognize: Loose cap, wet dressing, pump alarms, fever, leakage, resistance, catheter migration.
priorities: Use the prescribed home-care protocol and know which findings require same-day or emergency help.
assessMonitor: Site/dressing, temperature, line integrity, infusion function, supply availability.
interventions: Keep emergency contact numbers and backup supplies available; protect the line during bathing/activity.
medicationSafety: Do not improvise flushing concentrations, connectors, or infusion settings when equipment fails.
teaching: Demonstrate hand hygiene, connector disinfection, dressing protection, and emergency actions using the home program's exact instructions.
delegationScope: Home infusion tasks require training and jurisdiction/facility authorization.
examTrap: Telling a patient to force-flush a home PICC that suddenly resists.
oneLinePearl: At home, line safety depends on clean technique plus a failure plan.
